narrative: The model estimated a 61.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt, so the admission decision reflects a predicted risk above a coin flip rather than a certainty of failure. Your application was denied because that predicted risk was high enough to outweigh the rest of your profile. The strongest factor was your third-year class-standing decile: you were in decile 2, compared with an average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 35.5, which was below the accepted-student average of 37.18 but nonetheless leaned in your favor, toward passing. The third factor was your first-year class-standing decile: you were in decile 3 versus an average of 6.0 among accepted students, and this again pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 was close to the accepted average of 3.23, and your full-time status and middle-income background did not emerge among the strongest drivers. Gender and race were not used in the prediction. To strengthen a future application, focus on raising your LSAT score and, where possible, showing improved academic performance or additional evidence of bar-exam readiness; consider retaking the LSAT, taking preparatory coursework, and discussing with an advisor how to demonstrate progress before reapplying.
